When you log in as your own user account, programs you run are restricted from writing to the rest of the system – they can only write to your home folder. You can’t modify system files without gaining root permissions. This helps keep your computer secure. For example, if the Firefox browser had a security hole and you were running it as root, a malicious web page would be able to write to all files on your system, read files in other user account’s home folders, and replace system commands with compromised ones. In contrast, if you’re logged in as a limited user account, the malicious web page wouldn’t be able to do any of those things – it would only be able to inflict damage in your home folder. Adding support for a CPU architecture doesn't change anything with existing CPU architectures and doesn't have much to do with security.

CPUs are "backdoorable" because of crap added to them that isn't a CPU function, such as the Intel ME/AMD PSP. These are sub-CPUs that run independently along with the main CPU and are inaccessible to the CPU's OS by design, but not the other way around. No OS can do anything about this, it's pure hardware. The sanctioned purpose is to provide "Lights Out Management" (access to the system when it is powered off or the OS has crashed) and things like "Protected Audio/Video Path" (DRM that can't be sidestepped by the OS).

Not helping things are things like FSP - FSP is proprietary code that has to run when the CPU first starts up (even before the BIOS/UEFI can do much). FSP binaries are provided by Intel and Intel does not say what they do (other than "initializing silicon") or allow reverse engineering. If the Intel provided FSP doesn't run not even the UEFI (which officially boots the system) can do anything. AMD's version of this is AGESA - it was opensourced for a while then AMD changed their mind.

Things like this are 100% a CPU vendor issue and not an OS problem.

Chinese CPU might have backdoors, but Linux can't do anything about what happens in hardware before it is loaded no matter what the architecture. No OS can.
